Beer · Briefs for a brewer

Built for the table.

Beer designed to meet the food: designed to be crisp enough to cool the heat and round enough to hold a char. Nothing has been brewed. Each beer is a brief for a head brewer to critique, change, or reject.

Concept stage: there is no brewery, no restaurant, no truck and no menu for sale. Images are concept visualizations and illustrations, not photographs of NASHA. Alcohol is for adults of legal drinking age. Any future beer sales depend on licences we have not yet obtained.

The Core 5 beers

Five briefs, in plain words.

Nothing has been brewed and there is no recipe. These are briefs for a qualified brewer to challenge, written so a non-brewer can follow them. A brewer decides every process choice. Style-based concept visualization: any glass drawn on this page shows the style, not a brewed beer.

Hefeweizen

IN DEVELOPMENT Not brewed yet

A hazy, golden German-style wheat beer with a tall, dense white head. Typically it smells of banana and clove, and it is soft and creamy rather than bitter.

Its job on the list
The proof beer: the one used to test whether the whole beer program is credible.
Flavour intent
Soft wheat bread, gentle banana and clove from the yeast, very little bitterness.
With food
Lively bubbles cut through rich or fatty dishes, the clove note echoes warm spice, and low bitterness stays out of the way of heat. Goat birria and butter chicken quesadilla are the planned first matches (ideas, not yet tasted).
Why it earns a tap, and what is undecided

It is the beer most dependent on yeast character, so it is the clearest test of whether a brewing partner can deliver something distinctive. Its short, warm production cycle may also free tank time.

The brewer decides the yeast strain, fermentation temperature and pitch, whether a rest step is worth it, open or closed fermentation, how much haze and sediment to keep, and the pass/fail thresholds for each proof. Any clarifying aid must be free of animal products (no isinglass; nothing from beef or pork).

Under the proposed test rule this is the proof beer, judged on six things (credibility, difference from the others, repeat drinkability, food fit, fermentation reliability, taproom appeal) with four outcomes: continue, revise, de-prioritise or remove. A brewer sets the thresholds, and a Hefeweizen failure would not by itself stop the other pilots. The proposed test rule is not yet confirmed. Contains wheat and gluten; no gluten-free claim.

Mexican-Style Lager

IN DEVELOPMENT Not brewed yet

A pale, very clear, light and fairly dry lager with a small white head. It is made to be crisp and easy to drink cold.

Its job on the list
The everyday session beer for chile-forward food, and the planned largest share of volume.
Flavour intent
Light cracker-like malt, clean and dry, bitterness kept low so it does not push heat higher.
With food
Cold, light and low in bitterness, so it gives relief from heat without adding to it. Chicken 65 totopos is the planned first match (an idea, not yet tasted); it is expected to look thin beside very rich dishes like goat birria.
Why it earns a tap, and what is undecided

Chile-forward food needs a refreshing default, and a clean easy beer gives guests a simple starting point.

The brewer decides whether any corn or grits earns its place, how long to lager, the water treatment, protection against light damage, and where in the style range the bitterness sits. Whether to list it AND the Pilsner or only one is a real open question: they may draw different guests or the same guests, they may suit different foods or the same foods, the Pilsner may need more tank time, each may take sales from the other, and the tap slot might have a better use. No answer is given here; the evidence (tastings, brewer input, sales) does not exist yet.

Vienna Amber

IN DEVELOPMENT Not brewed yet

A clear copper-amber lager with an off-white head, medium body and a toasted-bread malt flavour. It has no roasted or burnt taste.

Its job on the list
The pairing workhorse for charred, smoky and slow-cooked dishes.
Flavour intent
Toasted bread crust and a little light caramel, clean, not sweet.
With food
The toasty malt meets char and smoke and bridges to rich sauces. Goat birria and butter chicken quesadilla are the planned matches (ideas, not yet tasted); sweetness could become cloying with some dishes.
Why it earns a tap, and what is undecided

It gives the list a darker, malty choice that is not heavy, and it is the most different from the lighter lagers.

The brewer decides the malt mix and balance so it stays dry rather than sweet, the lagering time, and the serving temperature (the traditional way is warmer than the cold default, so both should be tried).

Pilsner

IN DEVELOPMENT Not brewed yet

A clear golden lager with a dense white head, crisp and dry, with a noticeable but clean bitterness and a flowery or herbal hop aroma.

Its job on the list
The beer that shows a brewer's skill. It is the snappy, dry lager that the Mexican-Style Lager is deliberately not.
Flavour intent
Bready pale malt, a firm clean bitterness and gentle floral or herbal hops.
With food
Bitterness resets the palate between bites of fried and rich food. Gobi taco and chicken 65 totopos are the planned matches (ideas, not yet tasted); bitterness can also make heat feel stronger.
Why it earns a tap, and what is undecided

If a panel can tell it apart from the Mexican-Style Lager, it adds a second, sharper lager lane and a quality signal that flaws cannot hide behind.

The brewer decides hop choice and cost, how the local water suits the style, clarity and filtering, lagering time, and a warmer serving arm. Whether to list it AND the Mexican-Style Lager or only one is a real open question: different guests or not, different foods or not, the longest tank time against a style that may sell more, mutual cannibalisation, and whether the slot has a better use. No verdict is given; the blind side-by-side tasting and sales evidence do not exist yet.

Witbier

IN DEVELOPMENT Not brewed yet

A hazy, pale, soft Belgian-style wheat beer, traditionally brewed with coriander and orange peel for a light citrus aroma.

Its job on the list
A seasonal beer for the warm months, a citrusy choice for paneer, vegetables and char.
Flavour intent
Soft wheat and oats, light orange and coriander aroma, gentle and refreshing.
With food
Citrus lifts char and creamy yogurt and links to cilantro and lime. Paneer tikka taco is the planned match (an idea, not yet tasted); with some dishes the citrus could turn soapy.
Why it earns a tap, and what is undecided

It gives guests a lighter, fragrant option that suits vegetable dishes and has a natural place in warm weather.

The brewer decides the spice amount and timing, the peel source, how to keep the haze stable, how to avoid yeast cross-contamination with the Hefeweizen, and whether it is worth a slot. It overlaps the Hefeweizen as a wheat beer.

Mexican-Style Lager or Pilsner: a real question.

Both are pale, crisp lagers. The question is not only taste. Would they attract different guests? Go with different dishes? Need meaningfully different brewing and tank time? Would one take sales from the other? Nobody can answer that from a desk, so the plan keeps both and lets a side-by-side tasting and, later, sales decide.

If its bitterness is set toward the higher end, it starts to look like the Pilsner, which is why the two need a side-by-side tasting. Lime is not added by default. It is made from barley, so it is not gluten-free.

Why the Hefeweizen is the proof beer.

Under the proposed test rule this is the proof beer, judged on six things (credibility, difference from the others, repeat drinkability, food fit, fermentation reliability, taproom appeal) with four outcomes: continue, revise, de-prioritise or remove. A brewer sets the thresholds, and a Hefeweizen failure would not by itself stop the other pilots. The proposed test rule is not yet confirmed. Contains wheat and gluten; no gluten-free claim.

This is a proposal the founder has not yet confirmed.

Honest status

Not brewed yet.

No beer exists. There is no brewer on the team, no recipe and no licence. The first beers, if any, would likely be made with a partner brewery under rules we are still learning. Follow the path in The Lab.

NASHA is a future Indo-Mex brewery and kitchen in Austin, Texas, in development. Nothing is open or for sale, and no site has been chosen. Pictures are concept visualizations or drawings, not photographs of NASHA.

Name, images and allergens

The name was chosen by the founder; legal clearance is pending and nothing here claims trademark ownership. The word NASHA in the header and in some pictures is a temporary typographic placeholder, not a logo. Nasha means intoxication or addiction in Hindi and Urdu: we chose it for the feeling of being drawn in by food, craft and company, we will never present excess as something to admire, and cultural advisors will review the name and our language before launch.

Photographic-style pictures are concept visualizations made with AI tools and edited; drawings are illustrations. None is a photograph of NASHA, its food or its beer (about these images). Dishes are designs for testing, not served food; heat and vegetarian labels are design intent, not a certified allergen or dietary statement. Ask before you eat if you have an allergy. If you drink, drink responsibly; alcohol is for adults of legal drinking age.
